policies.summary: For eminent domain purposes, siting wind turbines or solar generating equipment is not a public utility activity, so neither utilities nor developers may condemn land for these facilities.

Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning; a merchant generator built after 2001 that is not in a regulated rate base may opt out of Kansas Corporation Commission jurisdiction, so no state body sites these projects.

restrictions.description: County counselor Austin Parker framed the pause under police powers to study public health, public safety, and welfare impacts of data centers, battery energy storage systems, solar energy, chip manufacturing, and cryptocurrency projects, on recommendation of the Brown County Planning Commission. Active. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-10 (motion by Chairman Heinen, seconded by Commissioner Pollock, motion carried unanimously per official minutes).

The county's Comprehensive Plan would generally allow incorporating provisions for data centers, BESS, and alternative energy technology into zoning regulations, but commissioners wanted a strategic pause to evaluate potential impacts on current and future property owners before adopting standards; no applications for these uses had been filed as of the July 2026 Planning Commission recommendation. Active as of 2026-09-23; the data-center-specific component runs through 2027-07-30, with BESS and renewable-energy components running longer (through 2028-07-30 and 2029-07-30 respectively) under the same resolution. Legal basis: Resolution # 073026, signed and passed 2026-07-30 by Chairman Kenny Roelofsen and Vice Chair Lynn Peterson, citing K.S.A. 12-741 et seq. and K.S.A. 19-101 et seq. police power; excludes uses already defined/enabled under Article 21 of the county zoning regulations and off-grid, on-site residential/commercial renewable installations.

A citizen-initiated petition (certified 2026-06-25 by the Butler County Clerk) sought to adopt an ordinance prohibiting 'high-impact' data centers (>10 MW peak load or >100,000 gal/day water draw) and Tier 2/Tier 3 battery energy storage systems; the City Commission voted to seek a declaratory judgment on whether the petition was a valid citizen-initiative subject, and adopted the interim moratorium to hold the status quo while that litigation proceeds. Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through 2026-11-30 absent further action. The underlying citizen-petition litigation (declaratory judgment sought from the District Court of Butler County) remained pending as of the sources retrieved. Legal basis: El Dorado City Commission resolution, adopted 4-1 at a special meeting on 2026-07-13 (resolution number not confirmed in sources retrieved), providing an interim moratorium on the development of data centers and battery energy storage systems.

Adopted alongside the data-center/BESS moratorium (Resolution No. 12-26); specific rationale not detailed in the source retrieved. Active as of 2026-07-31 (adopted 2026-07-23, after this dataset's 2026-04-28 coverage cutoff). Legal basis: Resolution No. 13-26.

County commissioners sought time to understand battery storage and data centers after presentations from Flint Hills Rural Electric Cooperative and Kansas Electric Power Cooperative; concerns included safety and protecting county residents. Active as of 2026-09-23; extended through 2027-06-01 by Resolution No. 2026-19 (unanimous 5-0 BoCC vote, adopted 2026-05-11), confirmed against the signed resolution text. No further Marion County commission action on the moratorium was found in news coverage through 2026-09-23. Legal basis: Resolution No. 2026-12, "A Resolution Providing for a Temporary Moratorium on the Acceptance of Applications Relating to the Establishment, Operation or Expansion of Data Centers within the Unincorporated Areas of Marion County, Kansas," citing K.S.A. 12-741 et seq. and K.S.A. 19-101 et seq. police power; passed and adopted March 2, 2026 (unanimous, 5-0; signed by Chairman Dave Crofoot, attested by County Clerk Ashley Herpich, county seal affixed). Extended one year by Resolution No. 2026-19, "A Resolution Extending the Temporary Moratorium...," passed and adopted May 11, 2026 (unanimous, 5-0).

The Neosho County Commission had already developed regulations for wind, commercial-scale solar, and battery energy storage, but had received no applications for data centers, nuclear power generation, hydrogen-based energy, or (further) battery storage facilities; commissioners wanted time to review and potentially adopt land development regulations for these uses before any applications arrived. Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through 2027-06-01 absent further action. Legal basis: Resolution R-26-7, "Providing for a Temporary Moratorium on the Acceptance of Applications Relating to the Establishment, Operation or Expansion of Data Centers, Nuclear Power Generation Facilities, Hydrogen-Based Energy Facilities, and Battery Energy Storage Systems within the Unincorporated Areas of Neosho County," adopted and signed 2026-05-19 by Chairman Gail Klaassen, citing K.S.A. 19-101 et seq. police power.

County commissioners wanted time to study data center and BESS impacts before making a firm policy decision; concerns included high electricity consumption, utility bills, and cooling water. Active. Legal basis: County Commission moratorium action [VERIFY resolution number from official minutes].

Zoning code allows BESS as a Renewable Energy System subject to Conditional Use review, but no BESS-specific regulations/standards exist. Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted by the Board of County Commissioners on 2026-03-11 for one year, through 2027-03-11, suspending BESS Conditional Use and Building Permit applications in unincorporated Sedgwick County while land development regulations are reviewed. Legal basis: Resolution No. 049-2026, interim development control suspending BESS Conditional Use applications.

County previously imposed a solar (SECS) moratorium in 2023 and expanded regulations in 2024; commissioners wanted more time before acting on two pending large-scale solar applications. Active as of 2026-09-23. Adopted 5-0 on 2026-06-17, in effect through 2026-12-11. Does not affect two solar applications already on file, expected before the commission in August 2026. Legal basis: Resolution No. 120-2026, interim development control suspending large-scale solar applications.

A surge of companies proposing data centers nationally prompted the city to act proactively and cautiously before creating permanent rules; this was reported as the first pause on data center/BESS development in the eastern part of Reno County. Active as of 2026-09-23; runs through 2027-05-26 absent further action. As of a July 23, 2026 follow-up report, the city had begun public-input meetings (an informational session held 2026-07-16) and was researching other cities' data centers as part of the moratorium-period study. Legal basis: South Hutchinson City Council ordinance, adopted unanimously at the May 26, 2026 council meeting (ordinance number not confirmed in sources retrieved).

Cherokee County, Kansas adopted Resolution R-27-2025 on Dec. 22, 2025: a nine-month moratorium on approving requests to use county roads, resources or infrastructure for commercial renewable energy projects (wind turbines or solar panels generating power for sale), cryptocurrency mining, data centers, battery energy storage systems, new or unpermitted landfills and transfer stations, quarries and nuclear energy plants, and a ban on constructing any of these in the unincorporated county during the term. Resolution 11-2026, adopted June 8, 2026, re-adopted the same moratorium through March 31, 2027, while the county weighs a comprehensive plan and zoning.

In May 2023, the Barton County Commission voted to require any solar farm to be 6 miles away from Cheyenne Bottoms—a wetland complex with significant wildlife—and placed a moratorium on commercial solar projects until the end of the year.
In August 2021, Cherokee County adopted a 1-year moratorium on wind energy development.
In response to NextEra Energy’s proposal to construct a wind farm, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development in December 2013, which lasted until April 2014.

In May 2023, the Franklin County Board of Commissioners unanimously approved a moratorium on the planning, establishment, construction, application for, or permitting of special use permits for wind farms in the unincorporated areas of Franklin County, Kansas until December 31, 2026.
In February 2023, the Harvey County Commission established a 6-month moratorium on commercial wind and solar projects.
Johnson County’s solar farm ordinance, which was updated in June 2022, sets the maximum area for a solar project at 2,000 acres.
The Kearny County zoning regulations provide that wind energy conversion systems must be set back at least 2,000 feet from any property line.
Labette County refused to sign road agreements with industrial wind farm developers.
In August 2022, Leavenworth County adopted a wind ordinance that sets a 1,500-foot setback from property lines and a 200-foot tower height limit for wind turbines.
Linn County adopted a moratorium on wind energy projects in June 2020, which was originally set to expire in December 2020 but ultimately extended through December 2021.
In November 2018, McPherson County adopted an indefinite moratorium on conditional-use permits for the construction of wind turbines.
On October 24, 2022, the Osage County Commission unanimously adopted a measure to prohibit any new commercial wind and solar projects within the county’s borders.
Pawnee County extended its moratorium on utility-scale commercial solar projects for three years.
Prairie County established setback and height limits for wind energy projects with resident permission.
In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county.
The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County.
In May 2023, the Wabaunsee County Commission adopted a 5-year moratorium on commercial solar farms, with an end date of June 2028

In June 2024, the Shawnee County Commission voted to ban community- and commercial-scale wind energy conversion systems in the county and unanimously approved a 1-year moratorium for solar energy conversion systems.
In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations.

The Pratt County zoning regulations require that wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from active residential buildings, although the setback can be reduced to 1,000 feet with the written permission of all affected residents.
In the fall of 2022, the Pottawatomie County Commission enacted a 1-year moratorium on utility-scale commercial solar projects.
In 2021, the county adopted a moratorium on commercial solar energy projects, which it indefinitely extended in August 2023.

In 2022, Douglas County adopted a solar ordinance that limits cumulative solar farm acreage in the county to 1,000 acres and requires solar panels and arrays to be at least 500 feet from any existing residences.

projects.description: Clearway Energy's proposed Rainbow Springs Solar project in Cherokee County, Kansas was stopped for now by the county's December 2025 moratorium on new large-scale energy projects. Clearway said it was disheartened by the decision, which it said stifles economic development and encroaches on property rights, and that it would keep working with the county and partnering landowners to find a way forward.
Local community members opposed a proposed 300-MW solar project near Cheyenne Bottoms, the largest inland wetland in the United States.
In 2015, Calpine Corporation proposed a 200-MW wind project on 30,000 acres on a ridge in Eastern Anderson County.
In January 2017, nearly 60 residents of Sumner County filed a lawsuit to challenge the county’s approval of a conditional use permit for the 60-turbine, 150-MW Argyle Creek Wind Farm.
In October 2022, Osage County Commissioners denied an application from Auburn Harvest Wind to construct a wind farm on 30,000 acres.

Shortly after the plans for a 103-MW Chisholm Trail Solar Energy Center project was proposed, in September 2023, the County Commission implemented a ban on utility-scale solar development for 6 months.
In March 2005, Spanish company Gamesa began developing a proposal for a 100-MW wind farm in northeast McPherson County.
The Hope Ridge wind project is a 334-MW wind project.
